title: Experts Push the Government to Finally Define 'Ultraprocessed' Food
summary:
What exactly makes a food "ultraprocessed"? Surprisingly, the U.S. government has never officially said. Now more than 100 science, medical and nutrition experts want that to change.

On Friday, the experts signed an open letter to the Office of Management and Budget urging the administration to release the first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed foods, often shortened to UPF. "It is critical that special interests not hold up this process," the letter read. It noted that most Americans have heard of UPF and wish to avoid them, but few understand them deeply, so guidance is needed.

The push has been building for a while. The administration first announced its effort to define ultraprocessed foods in July 2025, and in August the Department of Health and Human Services and the U.S. Department of Agriculture submitted a proposed definition for final review. The foods in question range from sugary cereals and sodas to burgers and store-bought breads. According to media reports, food company CEOs intervened in the definition's release.

So what is ultraprocessed food? The term comes from the NOVA system, proposed in 2009 by researchers in Brazil, which sorts foods into four levels based on how much industrial processing they undergo. Ultraprocessed foods have been through "extensive industrial manipulation," explained Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition professor at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who signed the letter. They are broken down and reassembled with cosmetic additives such as added colors, flavors and emulsifiers.

Studies have linked eating lots of these foods — often sugary, salty and fatty — to health problems including cardiovascular disease, obesity and Type 2 diabetes. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has connected Americans' overconsumption of them to childhood obesity. The public comment period on the government's definition effort ended on Friday.
why_it_matters: An official definition could shape food labels, school meals and health advice for millions of families. It would help people understand what they are eating and judge which foods are heavily processed.

keywords.explanation: Describes food that factories have changed a great deal, breaking it down and rebuilding it with added colors, flavors and other additives.

background_read: Governments publish official definitions and guidance so that food labels, school meals and health advice all rest on the same shared meaning.

The NOVA system, created by researchers in Brazil, sorts foods into four levels according to how much industrial processing they have been through, and ultraprocessed foods sit at the most heavily processed end.
An open letter is a public appeal that experts sign together to put pressure on officials to act.
Until the government releases its own definition, the word ultraprocessed stays fuzzy, and people cannot be sure which foods it really covers.
